# Retained-cap cone limits and a power-moment family

This source extends the physical retained-cap facet interface to a pointed
transverse cone. All conclusions are ordinary convex-geometric statements.
No mixed depth inequality or lattice-preserving localization is inferred.

Use d=m+k,1<=k<=d, a convex body F in R^m, x in int F, a closed pointed
full-dimensional cone Q in R^k, and v in int Q. In dimension m=0 use
counting measure on F={0}. Define J_Q, J_*(v), n_v as in Sections1--2 of
`candidate e70b63e0e6efe01c`:

 J_Q(b)=int_Q exp(-b.q)dq,
 J_*(v)=min_{b in int Q*, b.v=1} J_Q(b)=J_Q(n_v).

That source proves finite attained unique minimization, homogeneity
J_Q(t b)=t^(-k)J_Q(b), and -grad log J_Q(n_v)=k v.

## 1. The finite power-moment invariant

For any real p>1 put

 B_(F,p)(x)=min_a int_F[1+a.(z-x)]_+^p dz.               (1)

The parameter is empty and B=1 if m=0. Otherwise an inner ball at x
gives a coercive lower bound c|a|^p, proving attainment. Strict convexity
of the power on the common positive neighborhood of x for any two
parameters proves uniqueness. Differentiating the C1 integrand is
justified on compact F. At the optimizer a_p, set h=[1+a_p.(z-x)]_+.
Stationarity and multiplication by the affine factor give exactly

 int_F(z-x)h^(p-1)=0,
 int h^p=int h^(p-1)=B_(F,p)(x)>0.                      (2)

Consequently rho=h^(p-1)/B is a probability of mean x. If r=p/(p-1),
then int rho^r=B^(-1/(p-1)). For any other probability density sigma
with mean x, Holder gives

 1=int[1+a_p.(z-x)]sigma <=int h sigma
                  <= B^(1/p)(int sigma^r)^((p-1)/p).

Thus this rho is the unique minimizer of int sigma^r under the stated
constraints, and

 B_(F,p)(x)=
   [min_{sigma>=0,int sigma=1,int z sigma=x} int sigma^r]^(-(p-1)). (3)

The equality condition in Holder proves uniqueness. Infinite r-moment
competitors cause no difficulty. This is an actual mean-constrained
minimum-power density, not an assumed density ceiling.

## 2. Exact physical retained mass on the product cone

For P=F times Q at Y=(x,v), let T_P(Y) denote maximum finite dominated
mass with centroid Y. The optimum is finite, attained by one bounded
convex cap, and equals

 T_P(Y)=A_k J_*(v) B_(F,k+1)(x),
 A_k=(k+1)^k/(k! k^k).                                 (4)

To prove this directly, consider the nonnegative hinge integral

 G(u,-b)=int_(F times Q)[1+u.(z-x)-b.(q-v)]_+ dz dq.

Its finiteness requires b in int Q*. If b is outside Q*, along a cone
ray the hinge grows; if b is on the dual boundary, a null cone ray
translates a small ball around the source normal point v indefinitely
without changing its positive hinge. Taking z near x gives infinite
integral in either case. For b in int Q*, the elementary cone identities
are

 |{q in Q:b.q<=t}|=J_Q(b)t^k/k!     (t>=0),
 int_Q(A-b.q)_+ dq=J_Q(b)A_+^(k+1)/(k+1)!.              (5)

For the first, cone homogeneity gives c t^k for some c, and integration
of exp(-t) against its radial volume yields J_Q(b)=c k!. Integrating
the first identity over0<=t<=A proves the second. These identities
do not require a simplicial cone.

Set beta=b.v>0, n=b/beta, and a=u/(1+beta). Equations(5) give

 G(u,-b)=J_Q(n) (1+beta)^(k+1)/(beta^k(k+1)!)
                   int_F[1+a.(z-x)]_+^(k+1) dz.         (6)

All three optimizations separate. The unique normal scale is beta=k;
the cone direction is n_v; and the tangential parameter is a_(k+1).
Thus the unique hinge minimizer is

 u_*=(k+1)a_(k+1),   b_*=k n_v,                         (7)

and its value is(4). Its positive set is the actual bounded convex cap

 R={ (z,q) in F times Q:
            k n_v.q <= (k+1)[1+a_(k+1).(z-x)] }.        (8)

No positive part is inserted into the defining affine inequality;
where its right side is negative, its section is empty.

The volume of the q-section at z is A_k J_*(v)h(z)^k by(5).
Equations(2) make its total mass(4) and its tangential mean x. To compute
its normal centroid, disintegrate the cone along n_v.q=t. The exponential
law has expected q=k v, while its radial variable has mean k. Homogeneity
therefore gives mean direction v on the unit slice. The uniform cone
section n_v.q<=R has radial mean kR/(k+1); hence its normal mean is
kR v/(k+1). For(8), R=(k+1)h/k, giving conditional mean h v. Its total
normal mean is v, since int h^(k+1)=int h^k=B. This proves the cap's
centroid is Y. Its indicator is feasible, and the hinge inequality
int f=int(1+theta.(w-Y))f<=G(theta) bounds every feasible density by(4).
Therefore it is the actual optimum. Equality in that hinge inequality
proves uniqueness up to null sets.

The normalized cap marginal on F is

 rho_(F,k)(z)=h(z)^k/B_(F,k+1)(x),                      (9)

the unique minimum-L^((k+1)/k) probability density of mean x. The normal
conditional mean is h(z)v. For k=1, all statements reduce to the exact
quadratic facet theorem in
`candidate 449b4d02d42ead2a`.

## 3. Actual compact-body exposed-face limit

Suppose K is a compact convex body in R^m times R^k with exposed face
F times{0}=K intersect(R^m times{0}), and Q=cone(pi_normal K) is CLOSED
and POINTED. Fix x in int F and v in int Q. Then

 lim_(delta->0) T_K(x,delta v)/delta^k
                   =A_k J_*(v) B_(F,k+1)(x).           (10)

In normally dilated coordinates the actual centroidal cap indicators
converge in L1 to(8), and their probability marginals converge to(9).

Here are the limit details. Section7 of the energy cone source proves,
by actual convex interpolation and compactness, that K_delta converges
locally almost everywhere to F times Q, has a fixed ball about Y, and
is contained in D times Q for one compact tangential projection D.
It proves these facts without a product assumption on K. The source
ball bounds each actual hinge objective below by c|theta|. Choose a
fixed hinge with tangential parameter zero and normal parameter -ell,
ell in int Q*. Its positive region in D times Q is bounded, so it
uniformly bounds the actual minima above. Thus actual minimizing
parameters are uniformly bounded.

Along any parameter-convergent subsequence, Fatou gives a lower bound
by its full limiting product hinge integral. Finiteness forces its
negative normal coefficient b to belong to int Q*, by the ray argument
in Section2. Consequently the lower bound is at least(4). Conversely
the fixed optimum(7) has positive region contained in one bounded normal
range over D, because n_v.q controls |q| on Q. On that bounded set,
dominated convergence gives the upper bound(4). All actual minimizers
therefore converge to(7), by uniqueness. This proves(10), with the exact
Jacobian delta^k, without interchanging minimization and integration.

The limiting normal coefficient is interior to the dual cone. Hence
the actual minimizing hinge caps, for small delta, all lie in a common
bounded normal range over D. Local body convergence and convergence of
their cutting affine functions imply almost-everywhere indicator
convergence; the affine cutting plane and convex-body boundaries are
null. Dominated convergence then gives L1 and first-moment convergence,
and normalization gives the stated probability and marginal limits.
The point-face case m=0 uses counting measure on the tangent point and
ordinary volume in the normal coordinates throughout.

## 4. Exact comparison with the energy cone limit

The two ordinary limits have the SAME geometric cone factor J_*(v).
It therefore cancels in their ratio:

 lim E_K(x,delta v)/T_K(x,delta v)
   = [m! k!/d!] [(d+1)^(d+1)
                 /((m+1)^(m+1)(k+1)^k)]
                           E_F(x)/B_(F,k+1)(x).         (11)

For a pointed conical vertex m=0,k=d, this ratio is EXACTLY d+1,
independent of the shape of the cone and approach direction in its
interior. Thus the sharp ordinary E/T conversion loss arises at every
vertex in this proved conical class, not only at a simplex vertex.
For k=1 the ratio is C_d E_F/(2B_(F,2)), as already established.

The energy recursion preserves a lower-dimensional inverse-power escort.
The physical retained-cap recursion instead preserves the power-moment
family(1), with exponent tied to transverse codimension. These are
different induction data. Neither reduction has been shown to preserve
the lattice, all mixed cap inequalities, or a maximizing mixed center.
